title: I figured out how to get actually usable 3D models + animations out of GPT-6 Astra
author: Fearless_Brilliant51
selftext:
The entire character was modeled and animated from scratch in Blender.

This was the initial output from Astra after I gave it a reference image and asked it to create a 3D model for my character. From there, it was mostly a process of refining.  


https://preview.redd.it/mrgl2ouvndoh1.jpg?width=1000&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=c4b69ee9e9cb5afe6c49878d0b9de91b117bae9e

I discovered that Astra works much better when you give it very targeted prompts with as few distractions as possible.

Instead of giving broad feedback like “the face looks wrong,” I would take a screenshot of the exact area that needed fixing, give it the same-angle image from the original reference, and point out exactly what was different. When I did that, it would often fix the issue correctly in one go. Even if you are unable to describe the issue accurately you can point to the area and Astra will figure it out, as long as the images are focused on the area itself and not the full character.

The main workflow I ended up using was to first generate reference images of the character from multiple perspectives: front, side, and an angled view. From there, I would send focused prompts targeting one specific component at a time.

I was also basically spamming prompts through steering while it worked. I didn’t have to wait for every task to finish before giving it the next instruction. I could keep spamming things while it worked and it would work through them until all were fixed.

I generated the original character references and texture references using ChatGPT on High before giving them to Astra.

For animation, the biggest thing was getting proper keyframe references. You can ask GPT to generate a single reference image showing your character across all the important key poses of an animation, then give that to Astra to recreate in Blender.

That worked surprisingly well. The main problem I ran into was mesh clipping during the animation.

Unfortunately, I ran out of weekly usage before I could finish refining the run animation, so this is where I had to leave it for now.

Overall, the biggest thing I learned is that Astra gets significantly better when you stop giving it broad instructions and start isolating problems visually. Good references, matching camera angles, and focused prompts made a massive difference.

I’m currently porting the rest of the game over to Unity as well.

Follow me on Twitter if you want to see more updates on the game:

[https://x.com/code3ater](https://x.com/code3ater)

comments.author: call_stacks
comments.body: Literally the opposite of my experience, broad direction and few instructions give amazing results

replies.author: Fearless_Brilliant51
replies.body: Oh? could you share what you worked on

replies.author: call_stacks
replies.body: I replied off the cuff before bed lol but have been working on some games for personal enjoyment and learning. I tried to take a 2d game I made and make it 3d, first pass was to significantly define every little thing and every little plan and it took forever to just get thru one of my 10 plans, then decided I have 01-03 done, lemme just delete the rest and remove all the prescription for the game let Astra just learn the 2d game by source - and it worked waaay smoother, it was significantly faster and I had to do way less hand holding. Fwiw I do think it depends on the task you're doing, there is no one size fits all. And fwiw any vagueness is often going to give bad results, being specific without being prescriptive is where I found Astra shines, letting it be "creative" - outcome based target not prescribing how to get there.

replies.author: Fearless_Brilliant51
replies.body: I think that’s a matter of who has more knowledge over the task at hand, you or Astra. 2D game dev capabilities on Astra seem to be extremely good, so that might be the reason why less is better in your case. But with 3D, you can work with Astra because it is now able to actually carry out tasks, whereas previous, less capable models would struggle to do tasks regardless of how much handholding you provide. But it’s still pretty subpar, so more often than not, whatever it spits out will be below your vision, which is the reason why more handholding is required. But that’s just my guess.

replies.author: Fearless_Brilliant51
replies.body:
I’m not sure why Astra is performing better with less in your case. If I were to guess, I’m assuming maybe your approach was to apply a direct translation for the game from 2D to 3D, whereas you would have to alter the game to actually adjust for the game feel and other differences.

I mostly had to micromanage for the 3D modeling and animation. I have a pretty clear vision of what I want my game to look and feel like, so I would need to outline those specifics, or the output would be below my expected results.

comments.author: addr0x414b
comments.body: Could you please tell me how much usage this costs? I'm considering upgrading to pro specifically to be able to make models for games. But if I can only make one model per day, then I'll just hold off until it gets better/cheaper

replies.author: Fearless_Brilliant51
replies.body: I was working on the pro plan and it took me about 30% weekly usage to get this model + animation done from scratch. It's not worth making detailed models with more complex shapes with Astra because its just not there yet. If that's what you wanna go for you can use Tripo to generate the model and animate it with Astra. If you're going for simpler 3D models I would suggest using Astra, I personally don't like the way the mesh and characters look when generated from Tripo.

replies.author: TraditionalHornet818
replies.body: Bro 5x or 20x? Cuz i find it insane it took 30 percent usage on 20 to do this, you need to make a blender skill

replies.author: Fearless_Brilliant51
replies.body: It was 5x, I was having most trouble getting the mesh and textures right

replies.author: TraditionalHornet818
replies.body: Using plan mode ask it to build a blender skill using everything it learned in that task, also as part of the skill creation have it perform research on blender mesh, animation, textures, etc. Also in that plan tell it to plan your next 3d model and as part of the plan update the skill with what it learns. Then implement it and by the end you should have a blender skill that works really good, emphasize that the model, animation, mesh and textures should be final production level quality.
